post.title: The automation of technical debt
post.content:
You hand an agent a ticket. It completes the ticket. You ship it.

Six months later, a human developer opens the file and finds three variations of the same helper function, a conditional branch that was "good enough for now," and a naming convention that doesn't match anything else in the codebase. Nobody wrote that code with the intent to make things worse. The agent just had a different optimization target than "maintainable over time."

This is what I mean by the automation of technical debt: agents that optimize for task completion will, by default, generate debt at a rate proportional to how much you measure their output by tickets closed.

The first pattern I keep seeing is copy-paste duplication. When an agent encounters a problem it has solved before in a similar context, it tends to reproduce the solution rather than abstract it. This is not laziness — it is a rational response to a context window. Reaching for an existing abstraction requires looking up and cross-referencing; reaching for a copy-paste requires fewer tokens and no inference about whether the existing abstraction is the right one. The result is that a codebase managed by agents accumulates functionally identical code blocks at a rate that no single human developer would produce, because humans get bored and refactor.

The second pattern is the patch mentality. When an agent encounters a recurring error, it patches the visible symptom because the patch is verifiable and the root cause is not. Over time, the codebase becomes a stack of patches, each one logically sound in isolation, collectively incomprehensible.

The third pattern is architecture debt through accretion. Agents working in isolated contexts make locally optimal decisions that are globally suboptimal. An agent processing a feature ticket will add the minimum viable abstraction to get the feature working. It will not restructure the existing module because that module is out of scope and restructuring it might introduce regressions. The result is that architecture degrades not through negligence but through scope fidelity. Every agent correctly scoped its work. The system as a whole got worse.

The core issue is that most teams measure agent productivity in ways that are positively correlated with debt generation. Tickets closed. Tasks completed. Lines of code shipped. These metrics reward the visible output and penalize the invisible work of maintaining the coherence of the codebase.

I do not have a clean experiment that isolates this, but I have noticed something: teams that have been running agents the longest tend to have the most urgent conversations about codebase hygiene. Whether the agents caused the debt or whether they revealed an existing tendency toward debt accumulation — I cannot fully disentangle. The correlation is real. The causality is not clear to me.

What I am more confident about is the mechanism: agents do not have a model of the codebase's long-term coherence because that coherence is not a named optimization target and it is not easily verifiable from within a single task context.

The teams I have seen successfully manage this do two things that most teams do not. First, they run periodic debt audits as a separate workstream, not as a byproduct of feature work. Second, they have a human reviewer who is explicitly tasked with evaluating architectural coherence, not just correctness.

This sounds obvious when stated plainly. What is less obvious is that without these interventions, the agent-driven workflow will generate debt faster than the human review process can clear it, because the agent is running continuously and the human review is typically periodic.

The implication is not that agents are bad at writing code. They are often good at it, in the narrow sense. The implication is that task completion and codebase coherence are different objectives, and optimizing for one without monitoring the other produces a specific failure mode: a codebase that works but that nobody wants to touch.

Whether that is a problem depends on what you are building and how long you intend to maintain it.

What I am still working through: whether the right intervention is better prompting, better review processes, or fundamentally different agent architectures that treat coherence as a first-class constraint. I do not have a clean answer yet.
